newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Rumors cloud picture at Mexico's Televisa.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rumors cloud picture at Mexico's Televisa.

text.p: Like one of its trademark soap operas, Mexico's Grupo Televisa SA has been cloaked in drama and intrigue ever since the death of its powerful chairman threw the future of the huge media company in doubt.

Rumors of high-level changes in the company and clashes between rival groups of shareholders have mounted in the past few days, after last week's death of Televisa's legendary leader Emilio Azcarraga Milmo.

The rumors have sent shivers through the company's stock price, which on Tuesday was down 20 centavos to 100 pesos in late trade on the Mexican Bolsa. Analysts said the stock price has been hit at a time when the company is expected to report impressive first quarter earnings.
Televisa, the Spanish-speaking world's largest entertainment company, should clear up part of the mystery at its annual shareholders meeting on Wednesday in Mexico City.
But the meeting may not answer all the questions left in the absence of Azcarraga, a powerful businessman known as "The Tiger" who ran the firm for 25 years.

Mexico City's Reforma newspaper reported on Tuesday that current chairman Guillermo Canedo White would be replaced within the next few months or year by company president Emilio Azcarraga Jean, Azcarraga Milmo's son.
Televisa officials were not available for comment on the report.
When Azcarraga Milmo stepped down in late February ahead of his death, he appointed Canedo White, the respected former company CFO, as chairman and his son as president and chief executive officer.

The move was widely seen at the time as a bid to allow Canedo White to be the public face of the company and guide the 29-year-old Azcarraga Jean until he was ready to formally take power without scaring away investors.
Analysts said that although Canedo White shares power with Azcarraga Jean, there has never been much doubt about who the real successor was at the family-run firm.
But Reforma and other reports suggested Canedo White, 37, could be forced from the post sooner than expected, relegated to a less important role.

El Economista newspaper reported on Friday that a power struggle had broken out between Canedo White and Azcarraga Jean. But Reforma on Tuesday said the feud was really between Canedo White and Alejandro Burillo, Azcarraga Milmo's nephew, former Televisa vice-chairman and holder of a reported 15 percent of company voting shares.
"The real unknown in my mind is Alejandro Burrillo," said Francisco Rivero, an analyst at Valores Finamex in New York.
Rivero said he doubted reports of a battle between Canedo White and Azcarraga Jean, but said he assumed that at some point Burillo might re-enter Televisa's picture.
Burillo was forced from Televisa after the company's 1996 broadcast of an unedited video of a peasant massacre forced the resignation of a leading politician and angered the government.

Adding to the problem is the fact that few people know exactly who has how many voting shares in the company because two of the holding companies that own Televisa stock, Televicentro and Grupo Alameda, are privately held.
The Azcarraga family reportedly owns at least 50 percent, Burillo about 15 percent, the Aleman family about 14 percent and the Canedo White family some 10 percent.
Worry about the succession at Televisa could be blunted by the expected unveiling on Wednesday of a new executive committee which would have some decision-making power.

Analysts expect the committee to be made up of current executives such as Azcarraga Jean, Canedo White and Jaime Davila, plus some outside businessmen that are considered heavyweights in the world of Mexican business.
